*Disclosure: since this is an older project and I want to move forward, this blog post was generated by AI using my original report and documentation of the project.*

**TL;DR:** I built three ray tracing acceleration structures on top of an existing C++ path tracer - a median-split BVH, a BVH with the Surface Area Heuristic (SAH), and a Uniform Grid with 3D-DDA traversal - then spent way too long throwing dense meshes, sparse scenes, and cluttered scenes at all three to see which one actually wins. Turns out there's no universal winner, just a really satisfying tradeoff curve.

**Tech:** C++17, OpenMP

## The Goal

Ray tracing is expensive because, naively, every ray gets tested against every single primitive in the scene. For a few hundred triangles that's annoying. For the 871,306-triangle dragon mesh I ended up decimating down to a "manageable" 17,426 triangles, that's a non-starter. Acceleration structures fix this by letting a ray discard the parts of the scene it obviously isn't going to hit, instead of brute-forcing through everything.

The question I actually cared about wasn't whether acceleration structures help - obviously they do - it was which structure wins, and under what conditions it stops winning.

*Note: this was built on top of an existing Monte Carlo path tracer (physically-based and Phong materials, stratified sampling, Russian roulette - the usual RTIOW-lineage feature set), specifically [valentecaio's raytracer](https://github.com/valentecaio/raytracer).*

## The Journey

#### Building the Three

I implemented:

- **BVH (median split):** a binary tree, recursively split along the longest axis at the midpoint. Simple, cheap to build, and honestly more competitive than I expected going in.
- **BVH-SAH:** same tree, but instead of just picking the midpoint, the split point comes from minimizing a cost function based on child bounding box surface areas and primitive counts. More expensive to build, better tree.
- **Grid + 3D-DDA:** a uniform grid sized so each cell holds roughly one primitive on average (using `∛(primitive count)` cells per axis), traversed with the classic Amanatides & Woo DDA algorithm - basically walking the ray cell-by-cell like a voxel raymarch.

To actually compare these fairly instead of going off vibes, I instrumented the renderer to track average/min/peak traversal steps and intersection tests per ray. "It feels faster" is not a metric I trust.

#### Traversal vs. Intersection Is a Tradeoff, Not a Ranking

This is the part I actually enjoyed. On the dense dragon mesh, the two structures diverge in exactly opposite directions. The Grid needs way fewer traversal steps - as low as **~1.1 per ray** on average - because it's just walking linearly through space. But it racks up thousands of intersection tests per ray, since triangles pile up unevenly across cells. The BVH does the opposite: deeper traversal (up to **~33 steps** on average) but almost trivial intersection counts (under 1 on average), because it keeps subdividing until each leaf holds basically nothing.

Since intersection tests are by far the more expensive operation, BVH wins here. But not everywhere:

- **Dense single object (Stanford Bunny, control scene):** BVH dominates - it wraps a tight box around the mesh and skips the surrounding void almost for free.
- **Sparse scene (two bunnies far apart):** Same story, even more pronounced. The BVH's root node splits cleanly into "left bunny, right bunny," so a ray down the middle terminates almost instantly.
- **Dense, uniformly-distributed geometry (7,000 overlapping quads):** This is where it got fun. The BVH's traversal cost spikes to **~74 steps** on average because overlapping bounding boxes mean it can no longer cleanly send a ray down just one branch. The Grid finally gets to show off here - evenly distributed objects are its best case. But even in this scenario BVH still wins on total cost, because its intersection tests stay cheap (**~0.3-0.5 avg**) while the Grid's blow up (**~40+ avg**). BVH is basically betting "I'll pay more up front in traversal to guarantee I barely touch any triangles," and that bet keeps paying off even in its own worst case.

And SAH, predictably, just makes the BVH's traversal cheaper still - down to **~3.7 average** on one dragon viewpoint, versus **~18** for median-split - without touching intersection counts at all, since it's visiting the same leaves, just getting there via a better-organized path.

## Final Thoughts

If I had to sum up the whole exercise in one sentence: space partitioning (Grid) is cheap to traverse but blind to how geometry clusters, while object partitioning (BVH) pays more per traversal step in exchange for near-perfect intersection efficiency - and in every scene I tested, that trade was worth making, even in the Grid's best-case scenario. SAH is basically "BVH, but it also thought about where to cut."

Some AI assistance (Claude Code) went into debugging, code cleanup, and parts of the DDA traversal - that's disclosed properly in the repo README, because I think that matters. Done together with **Angelo Patanè** as part of an Advanced Graphics course - he handled the Grid implementation and instrumentation, I handled BVH/BVH-SAH and most of the analysis. Aside from the write-up, there's still more I want to push on here: more scene types, maybe a look at how these hold up with instancing, and eventually getting this onto the GPU where the traversal/intersection tradeoff probably looks completely different again.
